title: Study Design I — Observational Designs — Test

mcqs.q: A research study design is best described as:
opts: A framework and blueprint for how the researcher collects, measures and analyzes data
The statistical test chosen after data collection
The ethical approval document
The list of variables measured in a study
mcqs.explain: It is the method or process by which researchers organize their projects so the research answers the question at hand.

mcqs.q: An exposure variable is:
opts: A risk factor or characteristic that participants already have, which the researcher only observes and measures
A treatment deliberately assigned by the researchers
The clinical event that develops as a consequence
A characteristic describing the demographic profile only
mcqs.explain: It is the independent or predictor variable, and the researcher does not assign it.

mcqs.q: In a study of stroke prevention in adults with hypertension, smoking and pre-existing beta-blocker use are:
opts: Exposure variables
Intervention variables
Outcome variables
Confounding variables by definition
mcqs.explain: They are characteristics participants already have, which the researcher observes rather than assigns.

mcqs.q: An intervention variable is:
opts: A treatment, procedure or action deliberately assigned to participants by the researchers
A risk factor participants already have
The outcome that develops as a consequence
A background demographic characteristic
mcqs.explain: It is part of an experimental study such as a randomized controlled trial.

mcqs.q: The key difference between an exposure and an intervention is that:
opts: With an exposure the researcher observes what already happened; with an intervention the researcher assigns what will happen
An exposure is always harmful and an intervention always beneficial
Exposures are measured and interventions are estimated
An exposure is a dependent variable and an intervention is independent
mcqs.explain: Both are independent or predictor variables; only the researcher's role differs.

mcqs.q: The outcome variable is:
opts: The clinical event, health state or measurement that develops as a consequence of the exposure or intervention
The risk factor whose effect is being studied
The treatment assigned by the research team
The inclusion criterion for the sample
mcqs.explain: It is what researchers measure to see if the predictor variable made a difference.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a stated consideration when choosing a study design?
opts: The likely impact factor of the publishing journal
The aim of the study
The resources available — time, personnel and finance
Ethical considerations — participant safety and regulatory approval
mcqs.explain: The advantages and disadvantages of each design are the fourth consideration.

mcqs.q: Which design belongs to the DESCRIPTIVE observational group?
opts: Case series
Case-control
Cohort
Randomized controlled trial
mcqs.explain: The descriptive group is case report, case series, correlation (ecological) and survey (cross-sectional).

mcqs.q: Which study design appears in BOTH the descriptive and the analytic observational columns?
opts: Cross-sectional
Case report
Cohort
Case-control
mcqs.explain: A cross-sectional study can either describe a population or test associations.

mcqs.q: Both diagnostic and therapeutic interventional designs may be called:
opts: A clinical trial
A cohort study
An ecological study
A case series
mcqs.explain: The interventional group listed is preventive, diagnostic and therapeutic.

mcqs.q: In an observational study:
opts: The researcher documents a naturally occurring relationship and does not intervene
The researcher assigns participants to treatment groups
Randomization is always used
A placebo is always required
mcqs.explain: The exposure has already been decided naturally or by some other factor.

mcqs.q: Comparing the incidence of lung cancer in smokers versus non-smokers is an example of:
opts: An observational study
An interventional study
A randomized controlled trial
A quasi-experimental study
mcqs.explain: The researcher does not assign smoking; it is observed.

mcqs.q: A descriptive study is designed to:
opts: Describe the distribution of one or more variables, without regard to any causal or other hypothesis
Test whether an exposure causes an outcome
Compare a treatment with a placebo
Calculate relative risk
mcqs.explain: Its types are case report, case series, cross-sectional and ecological.

mcqs.q: Which descriptive design uses AGGREGATED data for groups rather than data on individuals?
opts: The ecological study
The case report
The case series
The cross-sectional study
mcqs.explain: The first three collect data on individuals; the ecological study uses group averages.

mcqs.q: A case report is:
opts: The description of a patient with an unusual disease or the simultaneous occurrence of more than one condition
An aggregation of multiple similar cases
A comparison of cases with controls
A follow-up of an exposed and a non-exposed group
mcqs.explain: A case series is the aggregation of multiple, often only a few, similar cases.

mcqs.q: HIV/AIDS was first recognized through:
opts: A case report of disseminated Kaposi's sarcoma and a case series of young men with pneumonia
A large prospective cohort study
An ecological correlation across countries
A randomized controlled trial
mcqs.explain: It is the classic illustration of case reports and series generating a hypothesis.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of case reports and case series?
opts: They act as triggers, stimulating analytic studies to identify risk factors
They can test the presence or absence of an association
They control for confounding factors
They provide a direct estimate of relative risk
mcqs.explain: They also identify new cases, formulate hypotheses, and can supply cases for a case-control study.

mcqs.q: The fundamental limitation shared by the case report and the case series is:
opts: The lack of a comparison group, so they cannot test the presence or absence of an association
That they take too long to conduct
That they require a very large sample
That they cannot be published
mcqs.explain: The case report also rests on one person's experience, and the exposure may be coincidental.

mcqs.q: An ecological (correlational) study looks for an association between exposure and outcome:
opts: Across populations rather than in individuals
Within matched pairs of individuals
Between treated and untreated patients
Before and after an intervention in the same person
mcqs.explain: It uses averages for both exposure and disease.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of the ecological study?
opts: It is quick and inexpensive because it uses already available data
It proves causation
It controls for confounding
It links exposure to disease in a particular individual
mcqs.explain: Its second advantage is that it generates hypotheses.

mcqs.q: Why can an ecological study never link exposure and disease in a particular individual?
opts: Because averages are used for both exposure and disease
Because participants are anonymous
Because it uses only questionnaires
Because the data are collected prospectively
mcqs.explain: This is the core limitation of using aggregated group data.

mcqs.q: A confounding factor is defined as:
opts: A factor other than the studied exposure that disturbs the relation between the studied exposure and disease
The outcome being measured
Any variable measured at baseline
The treatment assigned by the researcher
mcqs.explain: Ecological studies lack the ability to control for confounders.

mcqs.q: In a cross-sectional study, exposure and outcome are:
opts: Measured at the same time in the study participants
Measured before and after an intervention
Assessed backward from the outcome
Followed forward from the exposure
mcqs.explain: This single feature explains both the advantages and disadvantages of the design.

mcqs.q: Cross-sectional designs are commonly used for:
opts: Population-based surveys and assessing prevalence of diseases in clinic-based samples
Establishing causation between exposure and outcome
Calculating incidence rates
Evaluating rare diseases
mcqs.explain: Prevalence, not incidence, is what a cross-sectional study estimates.

mcqs.q: A descriptive cross-sectional design mainly aims to:
opts: Provide a clear picture of the measured situation, reporting percentages, averages, distributions, categories or profiles
Test a complex explanation with regression models
Track how the same individuals change over time
Compare treated with untreated groups
mcqs.explain: Its results should be read as descriptions of the measured period and sample.

mcqs.q: An analytical cross-sectional design:
opts: Examines relationships between variables and may use regression to adjust for background variables
Only reports percentages and averages
Follows the same people over several years
Requires randomization of participants
mcqs.explain: For example, examining whether study environment, sleep duration and attendance are associated with exam performance.

mcqs.q: A repeated cross-sectional design:
opts: Collects data at more than one time point, but not necessarily from the same people
Follows exactly the same individuals over time
Measures exposure only once and outcome twice
Requires a control group
mcqs.explain: Each wave is a new snapshot, so it shows population trends but not individual change.

mcqs.q: A national survey asks a new sample of students every two years about reading habits. This design:
opts: Can show whether the population percentage reading daily has changed, but not how individual students changed
Can show how each student's habits changed over time
Is a prospective cohort study
Establishes that reading causes better performance
mcqs.explain: Individual change requires following the same students.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of the cross-sectional study?
opts: We can estimate the prevalence of disease
We can calculate incidence rates
We can establish causation
It is suitable for rare diseases
mcqs.explain: It may also be conducted before planning a cohort study or as a baseline within one.

mcqs.q: The “chicken-and-egg dilemma” of the cross-sectional study means:
opts: Because exposure and outcome are measured at one time, it is difficult to derive causal relationships
The sample size is always too small
Cases and controls are poorly matched
The follow-up period is too short
mcqs.explain: There is no way to tell which came first.

mcqs.q: The statement that cross-sectional data “deal with survivors” means:
opts: Those who died or were cured are not included
Only elderly participants are enrolled
Only treated patients are studied
Only incident cases are captured
mcqs.explain: This is one of the four listed disadvantages, along with unsuitability for acute short-duration and rare diseases.

mcqs.q: A case-control study:
opts: Compares people who have a particular outcome with people who do not, looking backward at past exposures
Follows exposed and non-exposed groups forward in time
Assigns participants to treatment or placebo
Measures exposure and outcome simultaneously
mcqs.explain: Researchers start with the outcome and look backward in time.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of the case-control study?
opts: It is suitable for rare diseases and requires few subjects
It is suitable for rare exposures
It provides a direct estimate of incidence
It is free from recall bias
mcqs.explain: It is also easy, rapid and cheap, can examine multiple etiologic factors for one disease, allows estimation of risk, has no attrition problem and faces minimal ethical problems.

mcqs.q: The case-control design is characteristically able to examine:
opts: Multiple etiologic factors for a single disease
Multiple diseases arising from a single exposure
Incidence in exposed and non-exposed groups
The effect of a newly assigned treatment
mcqs.explain: Examining multiple effects of one exposure is the strength of the cohort design instead.

mcqs.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of the case-control study?
opts: It is not suitable for studying rare exposures, and bias is more common than in other analytic designs
It has a serious attrition problem
It is very expensive and time consuming
It cannot estimate risk at all
mcqs.explain: No attrition problem and low cost are among its advantages.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the four listed types of bias in case-control studies?
opts: Attrition bias
Recall bias
Interviewer bias
Selection bias
mcqs.explain: The fourth listed is bias due to confounding factors, which should be controlled by the control group.

mcqs.q: Recall bias arises in a case-control study because:
opts: Cases, knowing they are ill, remember past exposures differently from controls
Interviewers question cases more thoroughly
Controls are chosen from a different population
Participants drop out during follow-up
mcqs.explain: The design starts from the outcome and looks backward, which builds this bias in.

mcqs.q: A cohort study selects individuals on the basis of:
opts: Being exposed or non-exposed, then follows them to see whether the disease develops
Having or not having the disease, then looks backward at exposure
A single measurement of exposure and outcome together
Random assignment to treatment or placebo
mcqs.explain: Groups are identified at the beginning, followed over time, and their outcomes compared.

mcqs.q: The difference between a prospective and a retrospective cohort is that:
opts: In the retrospective cohort the starting point is exposure in the past and the follow-up is also in the past
The retrospective cohort starts from the outcome and looks backward
The prospective cohort uses only existing records
The retrospective cohort requires randomization
mcqs.explain: Both move forward from exposure to outcome; only where the researcher stands on the timeline differs.

mcqs.q: Which measure can be calculated from a cohort study but NOT from a case-control study?
opts: Incidence rate and hence a direct estimate of relative and attributable risk
Odds ratio
Prevalence at one time point
Frequency of exposure in cases
mcqs.explain: Only a cohort starts from exposure and watches the disease appear.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of the cohort study?
opts: No selection bias, because exposure is assessed before the disease occurs
It is cheap and rapid
It is ideal for rare diseases
It has no attrition problem
mcqs.explain: Because exposure is assessed first, the outcomes cannot influence the selection of the exposure.

mcqs.q: The cohort design is characteristically able to examine:
opts: Multiple effects of a single exposure — smoking causing CHD, lung, mouth and oesophageal cancer, peptic ulcer and hypertension
Multiple causes of a single rare disease
Exposure and outcome at a single point in time
Group-level averages across populations
mcqs.explain: Multiple causes of one disease is the strength of the case-control design.

mcqs.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of the retrospective cohort specifically?
opts: The records are unavailable and incomplete, and it is not accurate
Participants may migrate or die during follow-up
It is the most expensive design
It cannot estimate relative risk
mcqs.explain: Loss of participants during follow-up is a limitation of the prospective cohort.

mcqs.q: The attrition problem in a prospective cohort refers to:
opts: Loss of participants through migration, death or lack of interest during follow-up, affecting the validity of the results
Loss of experienced staff
Loss of funding
Change in standard diagnostic criteria
mcqs.explain: Loss of staff, funds, changing environmental factors and changing diagnostic criteria are the other prospective-cohort limitations.

mcqs.q: Which pairing is CORRECT?
opts: Case-control suits rare diseases; cohort suits rare exposures
Case-control suits rare exposures; cohort suits rare diseases
Both suit rare diseases equally
Neither is suitable for rare conditions
mcqs.explain: This mirror-image relationship is the fastest way to choose between the two analytic designs.

saqs.q: Define a research study design and distinguish between exposure, intervention and outcome variables.
saqs.a: A research study design is a method or process by which researchers in any field organize their projects; it is a framework used in medical research to gather data and explore a specific research question, and it serves as a blueprint for how the researcher collects, measures and analyzes data, ensuring that the research addresses the issue or answers the question at hand. An exposure or independent or predictor variable is a risk factor or characteristic that participants already have or experience; it refers to the risk factor whose effect is being studied, and the researcher does not assign it but simply observes and measures it, for example smoking and pre-existing beta-blocker use in a study of stroke prevention in adults with hypertension. An intervention, also an independent or predictor variable, is a treatment, procedure or action deliberately assigned to participants by the researchers as part of an experimental study such as a randomized controlled trial, for example a new antihypertensive drug randomly assigned to 300 participants while 300 receive a standard placebo; the medication is actively controlled and administered by the research team for the explicit purpose of testing its effect. The outcome, or predicted or dependent variable, develops as a result of the exposure or intervention; it is a clinical event, health state or measurement that develops or changes as a consequence, and is what the researchers measure to see if the predictor variable made a difference, for example the incidence of acute ischemic stroke within five years measured as yes or no or as time to event.

saqs.q: Give the classification of research study designs and explain the difference between observational and interventional designs.
saqs.a: Observational designs are either descriptive, comprising the case report, the case series, the correlation or ecological study, and the survey or cross-sectional study; or analytic, comprising the cross-sectional, case-control and cohort studies. Interventional designs comprise preventive, diagnostic and therapeutic or intervention studies, and both diagnostic and therapeutic designs may be called a clinical trial. In observational studies the researcher is documenting a naturally occurring relationship between the exposure and the outcome being studied; the researcher does not do any active intervention in any individual, and the exposure has already been decided naturally or by some other factor, for example the incidence of lung cancer in smokers versus non-smokers, or comparing the antenatal dietary habits of mothers with normal and low-birth-weight babies. Interventional studies are experiments where the researcher actively performs an intervention in some or all members of a group of participants; the intervention could take many forms, such as administration of a drug or vaccine, performance of a diagnostic or therapeutic procedure, or introduction of an educational tool, for example randomly assigning persons to receive aspirin or placebo for a specific duration and assessing the effect on the risk of developing cerebrovascular events.

saqs.q: Describe case reports and case series, with their advantages and disadvantages.
saqs.a: A case report refers to the description of a patient with an unusual disease or with the simultaneous occurrence of more than one condition. A case series is similar except that it is an aggregation of multiple, often only a few, similar cases. For example, HIV/AIDS was first recognized through a case report of disseminated Kaposi's sarcoma in a young homosexual man, and a case series of such men with pneumonia. Their advantages are that they identify a new case or an unusual variation of a disease; they formulate a new hypothesis for disease occurrence; they act as triggers, stimulating the initiation of analytic studies to identify the risk factors of the disease; and cases included in the case series may be used as cases in a case-control study. Their disadvantages are that the case report is based on the experience of only one person; the exposure may be coincidental; the lack of a comparison group in a case-series report can either suggest or exclude an association which may or may not be present; and neither of them can be used to test the presence or absence of an association.

saqs.q: Describe the ecological (correlational) study design with its advantages and disadvantages.
saqs.a: The ecological or correlational study design involves looking for an association between an exposure and an outcome across populations rather than in individuals. Its advantages are that it is quick and inexpensive because it uses already available data, and that it generates hypotheses. Its disadvantages are that it cannot be used for testing the hypothesis, that is, it never proves causation; that it is impossible to link exposure and disease in a particular individual because averages are used for exposure and disease; and that it lacks the ability to control for the effects of confounding factors, which are factors other than the studied exposure that disturb the relation between the studied exposure and disease.

saqs.q: Describe the cross-sectional study, its three forms, and its advantages and disadvantages.
saqs.a: Cross-sectional research means studying a defined population or sample at one point in time in order to describe features, estimate prevalence, compare groups, or examine associations between variables; the aim is to capture a snapshot of characteristics, behaviours, opinions, exposures, outcomes or relationships as they exist during that period, and the design may be quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods, although it is especially common in survey-based and statistical studies. In a cross-sectional study the investigator measures the outcome and the exposures in the study participants at the same time; the participants are selected based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria set for the study, and once selected the investigator follows the study to assess the exposure and the outcomes. Cross-sectional designs are used for population-based surveys and to assess the prevalence of diseases in clinic-based samples. The descriptive cross-sectional design describes a population or sample at one point in time and may report percentages, averages, distributions, categories or profiles; its main aim is not to test a complex explanation but to provide a clear picture of the measured situation. The analytical cross-sectional design examines relationships between variables and may compare groups, test associations, estimate adjusted relationships or build statistical models using data collected at one time, possibly including regression to adjust for background variables. The repeated cross-sectional design collects data at more than one time point but not necessarily from the same people, so each wave is a new snapshot; it can show whether a percentage has changed in the population but does not show how the same individuals changed. Its advantages are that these studies can usually be conducted relatively faster and are inexpensive; they may be conducted either before planning a cohort study or as a baseline in a cohort study; they give information about the prevalence of outcomes or exposures, which is useful for designing the cohort study; and we can estimate the prevalence of disease. Its disadvantages are that it faces the chicken-and-egg dilemma, since this is a one-time measurement of exposure and outcome it is difficult to derive causal relationships; the data deal with survivors, since those who died or were cured are not included; it cannot be used in acute diseases of short duration; and it is not suitable for rare diseases.

saqs.q: Describe the case-control study, with its advantages, disadvantages and types of bias.
saqs.a: A case-control study is an observational research design that compares people who have a particular outcome, called cases, with people who do not, called controls, to identify factors associated with the outcome. Researchers start with the outcome and then look backward in time to assess differences in past exposures between the two groups. Its advantages are that it is easy, rapid and cheap compared with a prospective cohort; it is suitable for rare diseases; it requires few subjects; it can examine multiple etiologic factors for a single disease such as smoking, physical exercise, stress and blood lipids in coronary heart disease; it allows estimation of risk; it has no attrition problem; and it faces minimal ethical problems. Its disadvantages are that it is not suitable for studying rare exposures, and that the problem of bias is more common in case-control studies compared with other analytic designs. The types of bias are recall bias, interviewer bias, selection bias, and bias due to confounding factors, which should be controlled by the control group.

saqs.q: Describe the cohort study, its two types, the rates it yields, and its advantages and disadvantages.
saqs.a: The cohort study design is based on the selection of individuals on the basis of being exposed or non-exposed, and following them for a certain duration of time to determine whether or not the disease developed; groups of people are identified at the beginning, then followed up over time, and the outcomes of the groups are compared, usually over years or even decades. There are two types: the prospective cohort, which starts with normal people, whether exposed or the control group, and then makes follow-up in the future; and the retrospective cohort, which again starts with normal people whether exposed or not exposed and makes follow-up, but where the starting point is exposure in the past and the follow-up is also in the past. The following rates can be calculated from a cohort study: the incidence rate or absolute risk, the relative risk, and the attributable risk or risk difference. Its advantages are that it is of value when the exposure is rare; it can examine multiple effects of a single exposure, since smoking is a factor that results in coronary heart disease, lung cancer, mouth cancer, oesophageal cancer, peptic ulcer and hypertension; the incidence of the disease among the exposed and non-exposed can be calculated; it provides a direct estimate of relative and attributable risk; there is no selection bias, since exposure is assessed prior to the occurrence of the disease so the outcomes could not influence the selection of the exposure; and it allows testing the hypothesis. Its disadvantages are that cohorts are not suitable for the evaluation of rare diseases; that the retrospective cohort is limited because the records are not available and incomplete and it is not accurate; and that the prospective cohort is limited by loss of experienced staff, loss of funds, change in environmental factors, change in standard diagnostic methods or criteria of diseases, by the attrition problem in which loss of participants through migration, deaths or lack of interest during the follow-up affects the validity of the results, and by ethical problems, besides being expensive and time consuming.
